description:
We are Narvalis, a technology-driven team participating in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 in Salamanca, focusing on the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge.

Our team brings together interests in software engineering, artificial intelligence, data science, and space exploration. We value innovation, scientific curiosity, and collaborative problem-solving.
summary: Narvalis is a public web tool that turns any star name or sky position into a verified, reproducible answer from real NASA SPHEREx images: does it move, how far is it, does its brightness change, and can the result be trusted? For any coordinates it fetches every SPHEREx exposure from NASA/IPAC IRSA, plays them as a short movie with the predicted Gaia track, measures the source in each exposure, calibrates each exposure on its own Gaia field stars, and fits the motion and the parallax. Brightness is compared only between exposures taken at the same wavelength, so SPHEREx's 102 colours do not fake variability. Every result is checked against dozens of field stars and is reported as reliable or not. On the challenge targets it reproduces Barnard's Star's proper motion within 0.25% of Gaia, measures the distance of epsilon Indi B from SPHEREx alone (3.3 pc vs 3.69 pc), finds WISE 0855 only at 4.2-4.6 microns as physics predicts, and detects the variability of RW Aurigae. It works on desktop and phone, and every analysis is reproducible from its archive files.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Narvalis turns a star name or RA/Dec into a verified answer from real SPHEREx data. For any position it:

1. fetches every SPHEREx Level-2 spectral image covering it from NASA/IPAC IRSA (SIA2 + cutouts, up to 150 exposures), with their pixel flags;

2. shows them as a short movie (filmstrip, play/step, zoom) with the position predicted for each exposure date from Gaia DR3 (proper motion, parallax, radial velocity), plus same-wavelength difference images;

3. measures the source on native pixels in every exposure and calibrates each exposure on the Gaia stars of its own field, so the error bars are real;

4. fits the proper motion and, with no catalogue input, the parallax, giving the distance from SPHEREx alone;

5. compares brightness only between exposures at the same wavelength (SPHEREx sees a source in a different colour at each visit, so a naive comparison invents variability) and builds an approximate spectrum from the time series;

6. runs the same pipeline on dozens of Gaia field stars as controls, and labels every result PASS / CONSISTENT / POSSIBLE / NOT RELIABLE with the rule that was applied;

7. writes a reproducible dossier (archive URL and SHA-256 of every file, all parameters, software versions); one command re-runs it and checks that the result is identical.

RESULTS ON THE CHALLENGE TARGETS (real SPHEREx DR1 data)

- Barnard's Star: 136 exposures, total proper motion +0.25% vs Gaia DR3 (0.25 sigma).

- Epsilon Indi B: motion -1.0% vs Gaia; distance 3.3 pc (2.9-3.9) from SPHEREx alone vs 3.69 pc from Gaia, a 6.6-sigma parallax.

- WISE 0855-0714: detected only at 4.2-4.6 microns, as expected for the coldest known brown dwarf; motion consistent with the catalogue. Narvalis also rejects a background Gaia star the brown dwarf is passing in 2026.

- RW Aurigae: brightness varies x4.0 at matched wavelength; its photocentre shifts with wavelength (unresolved binary).

- R Draconis (Mira): saturated core; variability flagged as possible, measured in the unsaturated wings.

Control stars: 0% beyond 3 sigma in every field, in motion and in parallax (166 stars). When a result cannot be trusted (saturated stars, shifting photocentre) Narvalis says "not reliable" instead of giving a wrong number.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Anyone, from students to researchers, can check in minutes whether a star really moves, how far it is and whether it varies, with honest uncertainties. These are exactly the signatures a nearby cold brown dwarf or a "Planet X" would show: faint, red, visible only at the longest SPHEREx wavelengths, recognised by its motion and parallax.

USABILITY

Desktop and phone layouts, a calm dark interface, a guided tour, research mode (exact RA/Dec under the cursor, pins fixed on the sky across epochs), a sky map with the challenge targets, user-selectable field of view, per-exposure metadata and pixel flags, downloadable dossier/CSV/ZIP, a live status panel of the archives, and URL queries (https://narvalis.pitipo-app.com/?ra=133.795&dec=-7.245 or ?target=...) so the tool can be embedded in other sites. New SPHEREx data releases are discovered automatically.

TOOLS

Python (FastAPI, Astropy, astroquery, PyVO, NumPy, SciPy, reproject) for the pipeline and server; vanilla JavaScript, HTML and CSS for the web app; Aladin Lite for sky context; GridStack.js for the customisable desktop layout. 75 automated tests. Code: https://github.com/narvalis-labs/narvalis-spherex

LIMITS AND NEXT STEPS

Circular Gaussian star model on 6.2-arcsec pixels (an empirical SPHEREx PSF would fix the parallax of saturated stars); neighbours closer than one pixel cannot be separated; stacking exposures for faint movers is the next step. When the IRSA search was down, Narvalis kept working from its cache and used a Gaia DR3 mirror.

Narvalis is an independent student project, not affiliated with or endorsed by NASA, JPL, Caltech, IPAC or ESA.

AI ASSISTANCE

Code and documentation were written with the help of an AI assistant (Claude, by Anthropic), directed, reviewed and tested by the team. All scientific results come from running the code on public NASA SPHEREx and ESA Gaia data; no number, image or result was produced by an AI model. No AI-generated images, video or audio are used, and no NASA branding is used.

PROJECT LINKS

Download source code and data (ZIP): https://github.com/narvalis-labs/narvalis-spherex/archive/2abf5269c15770ca6361dc5f8331a047e9871fef.zip
